question: Several hours after vaginal delivery, a male newborn delivered at full-term develops tachycardia and tachypnea. His blood pressure is within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 79% in the right hand and 61% in the left foot. Physical examination shows bluish discoloration of the face and trunk, supraclavicular and intercostal retractions, and a machine-like murmur over the precordium. Bedside echocardiography shows pulmonary and systemic circulation are in parallel rather than in series. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Newborn develops tachycardia and tachypnea" -> "indicates possible respiratory distress" -> "blood oxygen saturation is low" -> "right hand saturation -> 79%

CHAIN: "Newborn presents with low oxygen saturation" -> "indicates potential congenital heart disease" -> "physical findings suggestive of shunting" -> "echocardiography confirms parallel circulation" -> "requires intervention to improve oxygenation" -> "Alprostadil is indicated to maintain ductal patency" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Tachycardia and tachypnea in newborn" -> "suggests inadequate oxygenation" -> "low oxygen saturation readings" -> "indicates possible right-to-left shunt" -> "machine-like murmur suggests patent ductus arteriosus" -> "echocardiography shows abnormal circulation" -> "Alprostadil is the appropriate pharmacotherapy" -> 85%
analysis: The clinical presentation suggests a diagnosis of transposition of the great arteries (TGA), characterized by parallel circulation and differential cyanosis (lower oxygen saturation in the left foot compared to the right hand). In TGA, maintaining a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is crucial for mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Alprostadil is a prostaglandin that helps keep the PDA open, which is essential in managing TGA until surgical intervention can be performed.
